definition.text: Model Management is this repo's own model-access contract: a caller submits a request naming a routing class -- never a vendor, model or endpoint -- and a routing layer resolves that class to one endpoint at call time. This repo's own current-state facts state the rule directly: "Callers request a class, never a vendor. Prefix carries the contract." What the class actually resolved to on a given call is a separately-named, currently-unrecorded piece of state in this repo's own architecture graph: "model version pin behind a resolved routing class - the exact member model and its version that a class resolved to on this call."

evidence.quote: Callers request a class, never a vendor. Prefix carries the contract.
model version pin behind a resolved routing class - the exact member model and its version that a class resolved to on this call

standards.role: the request/response wire shape this repo's own model-access adapter and every named swap candidate all speak, so swapping the adapter is a configuration change rather than a rewrite of the caller's request or response handling.
standards.covers: does not standardize routing-class semantics, fallback behaviour, or budget ceilings, and it is not backed by any governing body at all -- it is convergent practice, not a published specification: "In the LLM world, there is currently (Dec. 2025) no formally specified standard like HTTP or SQL that is standardized by a governing body. Instead, a de facto standard has emerged that is supported by most providers: the “OpenAI-Compatible” API."

evidence.text: This repo's own registry marks this standard's version 'unverified' for the same reason this source states plainly: nobody governs it.

tools.name: vLLM Semantic Router
tools.note: A genuinely different architecture from a fixed class-prefix map: it composes routing with policy, budget and reasoning signals into one inference layer, rather than resolving a caller-named class through a separate lookup.

evidence.text: Not part of this repo's own stack; cited to show routing-as-a-composed-layer is a real, different design from a prefix convention.

evidence.quote: composes routing, policies, reasoning budgets and workflow signals into a unified inference layer

landscape.text: This card's own class-prefix design is a narrower answer than what the wider field calls 'routing', which is treated as its own active decision layer rather than a fixed lookup table: "Infrastructure providers are adding routing rules. Agent companies are routing between frontier and smaller models. Research papers are proposing learned routers, cascades and verification loops." vLLM's Semantic Router is one production instance of that wider claim, folding routing, policy, budget and reasoning signals into a single composed layer rather than keeping them as separate lookups the way this repo's own prefix tables (F-a4-02, F-a4-03) do. Fallback is a related but separate axis: when a call's budget is exceeded or a model becomes unavailable, the sourced industry pattern is to retry against a fallback chain of alternative models rather than fail hard, which is the same 'budget exceeded' trigger this repo's own rail.4 Cost Management card also names.

evidence.quote: Infrastructure providers are adding routing rules. Agent companies are routing between frontier and smaller models. Research papers are proposing learned routers, cascades and verification loops.
composes routing, policies, reasoning budgets and workflow signals into a unified inference layer

When budget is exceeded or models are unavailable, systems can automatically retry with a fallback chain of alternative models, providing zero downtime and graceful degradation instead of hard failure.

usage.text: A caller submits an idempotent request naming a class and gets back a claim ticket rather than a synchronous guarantee of which vendor answered: "Callers request a class, never a vendor. Prefix carries the contract"; "Every externally-triggered action is safe to replay." Resolving that class to an endpoint is not a static lookup alone -- this repo's own architecture graph names free serving capacity as one of the inputs the resolution reads: "GPU and fleet capacity - free-class serving capacity as a routing input, alongside budget remaining and latency class."

gaps.what: This card's own subtitle names 'Providers' as one of four concerns, on a card whose own governing rule is that a caller never names a vendor: "Callers request a class, never a vendor." Whether 'Providers' describes the multi-vendor plumbing hidden behind the adapter (consistent with the rule) or reintroduces a vendor-facing concept the rest of this card's own contract forbids is not settled by the evidence gathered here.
gaps.why_it_matters: A card whose own subtitle appears to name the exact concept its own contract says a caller should never see is either a wording accident or a real seam (e.g. an operator-facing provider-management view that is legitimately different from the caller-facing class contract) -- and nothing in the evidence distinguishes which.
gaps.research_query: does any operator-facing (not caller-facing) surface in this repo name a specific provider/vendor directly, distinct from the caller's own class-only contract

gaps.what: This repo's own current-state facts record a measured incident in the routing configuration path itself: "A `LiteLLM_Config` row in Postgres overlays and replaces `router_settings` on every gateway load. Values written to YAML validated, reviewed correctly, and had no runtime effect."
gaps.why_it_matters: A silent override between the documented configuration surface and the config a caller's routing decisions actually run against is exactly the kind of drift that would make this card's own class-to-endpoint mapping untrustworthy without anyone noticing, independent of whether the mapping itself is well-designed.
gaps.research_query: has the LiteLLM_Config Postgres override (F-a7-04) been fixed, or does it still silently win over router_settings.yaml

gaps.what: 'Evaluations' appears in this card's own subtitle alongside providers, routing and fallbacks, but no evidence gathered here describes a model-evaluation practice (e.g. benchmarking candidate models for a routing decision) that is distinct from cap-evaluation's own scoring contract, which this reference model places on separate cards (6.2 Evaluation Data, 7.3 Evaluate (Blind)).
gaps.why_it_matters: If 'evaluations' on this card names the same scoring concept 6.2 and 7.3 already own, this card's subtitle claims a fourth concept that is actually someone else's, the same overlap pattern already found between rail.4 Cost Management and 2.2 Policy.
gaps.research_query: kb_index.py search "model benchmark evaluation routing decision candidate selection" -- does anything distinguish this from cap-evaluation's own scoring

gaps.what: This repo's own architecture graph already records the model-version-pin state as an unresolved gap in its own status field, naming the exact shortfall: twenty-five groups resolve a class prefix to a member model name, with no version behind that name recorded anywhere.
gaps.why_it_matters: A caller cannot reproduce or audit which exact model version answered a past call if the version pin behind a resolved class is not recorded at all -- this is a named, specific absence, not a general one.
gaps.research_query: does any harness or example record the resolved member-model version alongside the routing-class name it satisfied, for even one call

gaps.what: Fallback (this card's own subtitle) and budget-exceeded handling (rail.4 Cost Management's own subtitle) are the same trigger in the sourced industry pattern: "When budget is exceeded or models are unavailable, systems can automatically retry with a fallback chain of alternative models." Neither card's own definition states which one owns deciding the fallback chain.
gaps.why_it_matters: Two rail cards each plausibly own the same fallback-on-budget-exhaustion behaviour with no stated boundary, mirroring the Policy/Cost-Management overlap already found -- a caller could implement fallback logic twice, once per card.
gaps.research_query: does cap-model-access's own routing operation or concern-budget's own contract state which one triggers a fallback chain when a ceiling is hit
